diagnosticNotes: A rough surface does not automatically mean the entire pool needs to be replastered. We distinguish removable scale from etched plaster, isolated delamination, widespread bond failure, and ordinary cosmetic discoloration before defining the scope.

The empty-pool inspection matters because water can hide hollow areas, cracks, failed patches, damaged fittings, and the actual condition of the bond beam. Preparation should be based on what remains sound, not on one standard demolition package.

Resurfacing is also the right time to decide whether failing waterline tile, loose coping, old lights, suspect return fittings, or circulation problems should be addressed. Coordinating necessary work now can avoid cutting into a new finish later.

A good recommendation explains why a localized repair is unlikely to last when failure is widespread. It should also explain when a pool is still a candidate for targeted work, so the homeowner is not pushed into a full renovation simply because a new finish is easier to quote.
ownerChecklist: Ask exactly how much existing material will be removed, how hollow areas will be identified, and what shell repairs are included rather than assuming every proposal describes the same preparation.
Compare finish samples wet and dry, in sun and shade. Water depth, aggregate color, surrounding tile, coping, and landscaping all change the final appearance.
Confirm who controls the uninterrupted fill, startup brushing, early chemistry, filtration schedule, and first safe swim date. A strong application can still be harmed by a poor startup.
Request separate pricing for required shell work and optional upgrades so you can compare proposals without hiding structural needs inside finish allowances.

diagnosticNotes: A remodeling evaluation begins with how the pool is used now and what is not working. We then inspect the shell, bond beam, tile, coping, deck interface, drainage, plumbing, lights, skimmers, returns, equipment, access, and electrical conditions that affect the plan.

Tile, coping, deck, and interior finish meet at vulnerable transitions. Cracked grout, loose edge material, poor drainage, or movement should be understood before selecting finishes, because a cosmetic replacement cannot stabilize a failing substrate.

A Baja shelf or tanning ledge changes more than appearance. Depth, step geometry, reinforcement, plumbing, circulation, finish transitions, water level, bubblers, and local requirements must be coordinated as one structural scope.
Not every upgrade belongs in the same phase. We separate work that protects the pool now from comfort, automation, and design choices that can be deferred without damaging completed surfaces.

diagnosticNotes: Pebble should be selected for the actual pool, not from a small dry chip alone. Aggregate size, exposure, pigment, pool depth, sunlight, shade, tile, coping, and landscaping all influence texture and water color.

We check whether the old finish is sound enough for the proposed preparation or whether loose, hollow, patched, or contaminated areas require removal. The exposed aggregate cannot compensate for weak material underneath it.

Comfort is specific to the swimmer. Standard pebble has stronger texture and visible aggregate; mini-pebble can feel finer. Steps, benches, a Baja shelf, and high-contact areas deserve particular attention during sample review and application.

Color consistency depends on application, exposure, fill, startup, and chemistry. Natural aggregate has intentional variation, so the goal is a well-applied, balanced surface rather than the flat uniformity of paint.

For a pool used by children, older swimmers, or frequent barefoot guests, texture deserves the same attention as color. Ask to review steps, benches, and shelf areas specifically; a finish that looks ideal across the pool may feel different on high-contact surfaces.

Pebble can hide small visual changes better than a flat white surface, but it does not excuse weak water care. Calcium scale, poor startup, and neglected filtration can still change the look and feel of an exposed aggregate finish.
ownerChecklist: Compare standard pebble, mini-pebble, StoneScapes, and quartz by touching larger samples and viewing completed work rather than relying only on catalog names.
Ask what chip-out, bond preparation, crack repair, fitting replacement, tile detail, and startup service are included in the quoted finish price.
Choose waterline tile and coping beside the aggregate sample. Dark finishes, reflective glass, warm stone, and surrounding shade can shift the perceived water color.
Confirm the 28-day brushing and chemistry plan, warranty conditions, and who documents startup readings before the pool returns to routine service.

Select a quartz blend and prepare the surface
Apply the finish and complete tile or coping details
Fill, balance startup chemistry, and explain maintenance

Quartz blend and color
Chip-out, patching, and preparation

aftercare: Brush and filter during the initial cure according to the written schedule, including steps and benches where dust or early deposits can remain even when the deep end looks clear

diagnosticNotes: Quartz is an upgrade to a cement-based plaster matrix, not a waterproof paint. The evaluation still needs to identify hollow material, cracks, weak patches, stains, scale, fittings, and shell conditions that determine preparation.

The fine aggregate usually feels smoother than larger pebble, but blend, exposure, workmanship, and the condition of steps and benches affect comfort. Homeowners should compare actual texture, not assume every quartz finish feels identical.

Color and mottling are influenced by pigments, troweling, fill water, curing, brushing, and chemistry. We discuss natural variation before installation and plan startup to reduce preventable scale, streaking, and uneven hydration.

Quartz can be the right middle choice when classic plaster feels too plain and pebble feels too textured. It should still be compared against expected service life, budget, water color, hard-water maintenance, and surrounding materials.

The best comparison is not simply smooth versus rough. A homeowner should weigh how much visual variation is desired, how the finish will feel on steps and benches, how often hard water is managed, and whether the surrounding tile and coping support the chosen color.
ownerChecklist: Identify the exact quartz blend, base color, and included preparation in writing; generic references to upgraded plaster make bids difficult to compare.
View the sample wet and in backyard light, then compare it beside the planned tile and coping. Pool depth will make the installed water color appear stronger.
Ask who manages fill water, brushing, filtration, pH, alkalinity, calcium, and sanitizer during the first weeks, and request written startup instructions.
Confirm how stains, hollow areas, cracks, fittings, lights, and existing repairs will be handled before the quartz finish is applied.

aftercare: Monitor the water level after the repair with a repeatable mark or bucket comparison rather than relying on memory, especially during hot, windy, or unusually dry weather
Keep equipment operating on its normal schedule and check pump prime, baskets, valves, filter pressure, autofill behavior, and visible fittings for changes after the repair
Watch for air, wet areas, deck movement, staining, unusual water bills, or renewed water loss and record when each symptom appears relative to pump operation

whenToCall: The water level drops repeatedly beyond normal evaporation
The pump loses prime, the basket fills with air, or returns behave differently
Wet soil, deck movement, staining, or unexplained water appears near the pool
You are planning resurfacing and want to rule out an unresolved leak first
diagnosticNotes: Water loss should be measured before parts are replaced. A marked-level or bucket comparison, normal weather observations, autofill status, recent backwashing, splash-out, and the difference between pump-on and pump-off loss help define the next test.

Air in the pump basket points toward a suction-side condition, but it may come from water level, a skimmer vortex, a lid seal, a valve, or plumbing. Wet soil alone also does not prove which line or fitting is responsible.

Dye testing can help at a visible crack, fitting, light niche, skimmer, or suspected shell opening when the water is still. Pressure testing may narrow buried plumbing, but access and system layout determine what can be isolated conclusively.
Leak assessment should precede resurfacing, tile replacement, or deck work. A new finish can cover visual clues, while later plumbing access can damage recently completed surfaces.
ownerChecklist: Record the water level at the same time for several days, note weather and equipment schedules, disable the autofill only when safe, and photograph wet areas or air in the system.
Ask what the assessment can confirm, what remains a hypothesis, which tests are included, and whether a specialist or destructive access may be needed next.
Do not authorize broad deck demolition from one symptom. Request a test path that narrows shell, fittings, equipment, suction plumbing, and return plumbing in a logical order.
After repair, repeat the same controlled water-loss observation and monitor pump prime, soil, fittings, and the water bill so the result is verified.

It is included because its before-and-after sequence shows why water-loss questions must be settled before structural work, masonry, equipment changes, and a new interior finish are closed in.
projectExample.challenge: Cracked plaster, fading coping, and outdated equipment created overlapping visual and mechanical decisions. Conditions like these can obscure the source of water loss if a contractor assumes every drop is caused by the visible surface.
projectExample.response: Rivera Pools coordinated structural remodeling, StoneScapes resurfacing, glass tile, natural-stone work, and a Pentair smart pump. On any comparable renovation, suspected leakage should be assessed before that sequence so later testing does not disturb finished work.
projectExample.lesson: A real project does not become a leak case simply because it includes plumbing and resurfacing. The correct lesson is sequencing: document loss, narrow the source, plan repairs, and only then close the pool with new finishes.
